title: The Stuff You Should Know Doin’ Science Playlist: How the Scientific Method Works
summary: Stuff You Should Know playlist episode (Doin' Science playlist, entry about pre-scientific-method beliefs). Hosts walk through ideas people accepted before the scientific method: the four humors of Hippocrates and Galen; Eudoxus' circular, shell-based geocentric model (with Anaximenes' shells and Copernicus/Kepler's later correction); Philolaus' central fire and counter-Earth; the four classical elements (Anaximenes, Plato, Aristotle) versus Empedocles' elements and love/strife as attractive forces; Democritus' indivisible atoms and the void, later vindicated by Torricelli's vacuum experiment and Dalton's atomic theory; and spontaneous generation (van Helmont's scorpions and mice, Redi's muslin experiment, van Leeuwenhoek's microscope, Pasteur's sterilization), plus epigenesis versus preformationism. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about the 'a' versus 'an' rule before historic, and a request for a pro wrestling episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and framing
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on beliefs held before the scientific method and recap that the method tests hypotheses rather than relying on observation or philosophy alone.

segments.title: Four humors and humoral medicine
segments.summary: Humoral medicine, traced to Hippocrates and popularized by Galen, held that blood, phlegm, and black and yellow bile governed health via hot/cold and wet/dry qualities. Treatments aimed to restore balance, including bloodletting. Harvey's demonstration of blood circulation later undermined it, and it survives in Ayurveda.

segments.title: Eudoxus and shell-based geocentrism
segments.summary: Eudoxus of Cnidus proposed a geocentric universe with circular, regular celestial motion, modeled with nested shells, building on Anaximander's idea. The circular assumption came from the belief in perfect circles and the lack of non-circular math. Copernicus kept the shells, and Kepler showed elliptical orbits.

segments.title: Pythagorean central fire and counter-Earth
segments.summary: The Pythagoreans, through Philolaus, proposed that Earth, Sun, Moon, planets and an unseen counter-Earth orbited a central fire in circular orbits, with ten bodies in total. The model explained lunar eclipses through the counter-Earth. Hosts note the orbital periods and that modern astrophysics rules out a counter-Earth.

segments.title: Four elements and Empedocles
segments.summary: Earth, air, fire and water were treated as basic elements, with Anaximenes favoring air, then Plato and Aristotle adding ether. Empedocles proposed that everything combined from these four elements through attractive forces he called love. Observations like wood being solid, floating, and burning were used to support the theory.

segments.title: Democritus, atoms, and the void
segments.summary: Democritus proposed indivisible atoms moving in void. Aristotle rejected the void and favored the four elements. Torricelli's vacuum experiment and barometer in 1643 showed air had weight and that a vacuum could exist, and John Dalton later developed atomic theory in 1803.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts announce a break before the final topic.

segments.title: Spontaneous generation and epigenesis
segments.summary: Spontaneous generation held that life, including mice, scorpions and maggots, arose from non-living matter. Van Helmont gave examples, Redi disproved maggot generation with covers, and van Leeuwenhoek's microscope revealed microbes. Experiments by others were contested until Pasteur's sterilization work. Epigenesis and preformationism were the rival theories of reproduction in the ancient and early modern periods.

segments.title: Listener mail: a vs. an before historic
segments.summary: A listener's question about whether to say 'an historic' or 'a historic' is answered with a rule based on the initial sound of the word, and the hosts respond to a listener request for a pro wrestling episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the email address for listener mail and the iHeartRadio credit.
